hello.title: Hello, Fortran!
hello.summary: Write your first Fortran program and print text and numbers with print and simple formats.
hello.lesson.0: Fortran is one of the oldest programming languages, and scientists and engineers still use it for fast number crunching. Every program starts with `program` and a name, and it ends with `end program` and the same name.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `program hello` starts a program called `hello`. `implicit none` tells the compiler that you declare every variable yourself, which you learn in the next unit. Always write it as the second line. `print` writes one line of output. `end program hello` ends the program.
hello.lesson.4: After `print` comes a **format**, then a comma `,` and the values. The format `'(A)'` is a short text in single quotes with parentheses inside. The letter `A` stands for one piece of text. Text values go in double quotes, like `"Hello"`. Every `print` starts a new line.
hello.lesson.6: The format `'(A, A)'` has room for two texts. Fortran prints them right next to each other, so the space after `Fortran` comes from the first text. To print a whole number, use `I0`: the letter `I` stands for integer (a whole number), and `0` means "no extra spaces".
hello.lesson.8: Without quotes, `2 + 3` is a calculation and Fortran prints `5`. In quotes, `"2 + 3"` is only text. The star `*` multiplies. A format can mix text and numbers: `'(A, I0)'` prints a text and then a whole number.
hello.lesson.9: You will often see `print *, "Hi"`. The star lets the compiler choose the layout, and it usually adds a space at the start of the line. This course uses formats such as `'(A)'`, so you always know the exact output.
hello.lesson.10: An exclamation mark `!` starts a **comment**: Fortran ignores the rest of the line. Fortran is also not case sensitive, so `PRINT`, `Print` and `print` mean the same. Old programs are often written in capital letters.
hello.lesson.12: The name after `end program` must be the same as the name after `program`. Every text needs a closing quote, and a comma must separate the format from the values.
hello.card.0: `program name` … `end program name` frame a program
hello.card.2: `print '(A)', "Hi"` prints text and ends the line
hello.card.3: `'(I0)'` prints a whole number, `!` starts a comment
hello-1.options.0: It makes you declare every variable yourself
hello-1.explain: With `implicit none`, every variable must be declared. A variable that is not declared is an error, so typos are found early.
hello-2.explain: `'(A, A)'` prints the two texts right next to each other. There is no space because neither text contains one.
hello-3.explain: `7 * 6` is `42`, minus `2` gives `40`. `I0` prints the whole number without extra spaces.
hello-4.statement: Fortran is case sensitive: `PRINT` and `print` are different.
hello-4.explain: Fortran ignores the case of letters. `PRINT`, `Print` and `print` all work the same way.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Hello.
hello-5.explain: The format for text is `'(A)'`, with the parentheses inside the quotes. `I0` is only for whole numbers.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the last line of the program.
hello-6.explain: A program ends with `end program` and the same name as in the first line, here `first`.
hello-7.prompt: Build the line that prints 6, the result of 10 minus 4.
hello-7.explain: First `print`, then the format `'(I0)'` for a whole number, a comma, and the calculation `10 - 4`.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints One, then Two.
hello-8.explain: The program starts with `program` and `implicit none`. The `print` lines run from top to bottom, and `end program` comes last.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.explain: The text has no closing quote. Write `"Hello"`.
hello-11.explain: The name after `end program` must match the first line. Write `end program add`.
hello-12.explain: The first value is text in quotes, so it is printed as it is. The second one has no quotes, so Fortran calculates `8`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Declare variables of type integer, real, character and logical, and name fixed values with parameter.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Fortran you declare every variable at the top of the program: after `implicit none` and before the first statement. `integer :: age` declares a variable `age` for whole numbers. The sign `=` stores a value in it.
variables.lesson.2: `age = age + 1` is not an equation. Fortran first calculates the right side, here `36 + 1`, and then stores the result `37` in the variable on the left.
variables.lesson.4: `integer` holds whole numbers. `real` holds numbers with a decimal point, such as `2.5`. `character(len=5)` holds a text of exactly 5 characters. `logical` holds `.true.` or `.false.`, and the dots belong to the value. You can give a variable a start value in its declaration.
variables.lesson.6: Each type has its own format. `F0.2` prints a real number with 2 digits after the decimal point. `L1` prints a logical value as `T` for true or `F` for false.
variables.lesson.7: A `character(len=10)` variable always holds 10 characters. Shorter text is filled up with spaces at the end, and longer text is cut. `trim(name)` removes the spaces at the end, `//` joins two texts, and `len(name)` gives the length.
variables.lesson.10: Add `parameter` to a declaration to make a **named constant**. You give the value in the declaration, and it can never change. Trying to store a new value in it is an error. Several variables of the same type can share one declaration, separated by commas.
variables.lesson.12: All declarations come before the first statement. A declaration after a `print` or after `x = 1` is an error. Without `implicit none`, Fortran guesses the type of an undeclared name from its first letter, so a typo quietly creates a new variable.
variables.card.3: `'(F0.2)'` for real, `'(L1)'` for logical, `trim(s) // "!"` joins text
variables-1.prompt: Which type should you use to store `3.75`?
variables-1.explain: `real` holds numbers with a decimal point. An `integer` variable would lose the part after the decimal point.
variables-2.explain: `n` becomes `10`, then `20`, then `15`. Each line uses the value from the line before.
variables-3.explain: `word` has room for only 4 characters, so Fortran cuts the text to `plan`.
variables-4.statement: A variable declared with `parameter` can get a new value later in the program.
variables-4.explain: A `parameter` is a constant. Its value is fixed in the declaration, and assigning a new value is an error.
variables-5.prompt: Complete the declaration so the program prints T.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hi, Ada` with no spaces at the end.
variables-6.explain: `name` holds `Ada` plus 7 spaces. `trim(name)` removes the spaces at the end.
variables-7.prompt: Build the declaration of a real constant `rate` with the value 1.5.
variables-7.explain: The type comes first, then `, parameter`, then `::`, the name and the value.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Total: 7`.
variables-8.explain: `implicit none` and the declaration come first. Then `a` gets `3`, then `3 + 4`, and only then is it printed.
variables-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
variables-10.explain: All declarations must come before the first statement. Move `integer :: count` up, before `cost = 4.5`.
variables-11.explain: Logical values are written with dots: `ready = .true.`.
variables-12.explain: `d` is about `6.28318`. `F0.2` shows 2 digits after the decimal point and rounds, so you see `6.28`.
operators.title: Arithmetic and formatted output
operators.summary: Calculate with numbers and powers, learn how integer division works and control the layout of numbers with write and formats.
operators.lesson.0: Fortran calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply), `/` (divide) and `**` (power). The order is the same as in mathematics: first `**`, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Parentheses change the order.
operators.lesson.3: When both numbers are integers, `/` gives an integer and cuts off the decimal part: `7 / 2` is `3`. `mod(7, 2)` gives the remainder of the division, `1`. When at least one number is real, the result is real: `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`.
operators.lesson.5: `real(n)` turns an integer into a real number. `int(x)` turns a real into an integer and cuts off the decimal part. `nint(x)` rounds to the nearest integer. When you store a real value in an integer variable, Fortran also cuts off the decimal part.
operators.lesson.8: `write(*, '(I5)') n` works like `print '(I5)', n`. The `*` means the screen. Inside a format, each letter code describes one value: `I5` is an integer in 5 characters, aligned to the right. `F8.3` is a real in 8 characters with 3 digits after the decimal point. `1X` adds one space.
operators.lesson.10: A number in front of a letter code repeats it: `3I4` is the same as `I4, I4, I4`. When a number does not fit into its width, Fortran prints stars instead. `I0` and `F0.2` always use as many characters as the number needs.
operators.lesson.12: For numbers between -1 and 1, many compilers, gfortran too, leave out the zero before the decimal point with `F0.2`: `0.5` prints as `.50`. Use a fixed width such as `F4.2` when you want `0.50`.
operators.card.3: `write(*, '(I5, 1X, F8.3)') n, x` sets the widths
operators-1.explain: Both numbers are integers, so `/` cuts off the decimal part of `3.4`.
operators-4.explain: `10.0` is real, so the result is the real number `2.5`. `F0.2` shows it with 2 digits after the decimal point.
operators-5.explain: Fortran calculates from left to right: `9 / 2` is `4` because the decimal part is cut off, and `4 * 2` is `8`.
operators-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2.50`.
operators-6.explain: `real(a)` makes the division real, so the result is `2.5`. With two integers the result would be `2`, and `F0.2` cannot print an integer.
operators-7.prompt: Complete the format so it prints `Total: 42`.
operators-7.explain: `I0` prints the integer with no extra spaces. `I5` would add three spaces in front of `42`.
operators-8.prompt: Build the line that prints 2 to the power of 8.
operators-8.explain: The power operator in Fortran is `**`. The result `256` is a whole number, so the format is `'(I0)'`.
operators-9.prompt: Match the format code with its meaning.
operators-10.prompt: The program should print `3.50`. Which line has the bug?
operators-10.explain: `n / 2` is an integer division and gives `3`. Write `h = real(n) / 2` to get `3.5`.
operators-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Area: 6.00`.
operators-11.explain: The declaration comes first. `w` must have its value before `h` is calculated from it, and the result is printed last: `2.0 * 3.0` is `6.0`.
operators-12.prompt: Which format prints the integer `7` as `   7`, with three spaces in front?
operators-12.explain: `I4` uses 4 characters and aligns the number to the right, so three spaces come before `7`. `F` is only for real numbers.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, else if and select case, and combine conditions with .and., .or. and .not.
conditions.lesson.0: `if (condition) then` runs the following lines only when the condition is true. `end if` closes the block. The condition goes in parentheses. You compare values with `==` (equal), `/=` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.2: `else` adds code for the case that the condition is false. `else if` checks another condition. Fortran checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.
conditions.lesson.4: For a single statement there is a short form without `then` and `end if`: `if (x < 0) x = -x` changes `x` only when it is negative.
conditions.lesson.7: `.and.` is true when both sides are true. `.or.` is true when at least one side is true. `.not.` turns true into false and false into true. A `logical` variable can be a condition on its own. In old code you may see `.eq.`, `.ne.`, `.lt.` and `.gt.` instead of `==`, `/=`, `<` and `>`.
conditions.lesson.10: `select case (x)` compares one value with many cases. `case (1)` matches one value, `case (2, 3)` a list, and `case (4:6)` a range from 4 to 6. `case default` matches all other values. It works with integers and texts, but not with real numbers.
conditions.lesson.12: `=` stores a value and `==` compares two values, so `if (x = 5)` is an error. "Not equal" is `/=`, not `!=`, because `!` starts a comment in Fortran.
conditions-1.explain: `15 > 10` is true, so the first block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `7` is not in `1:3` or `4:6`, so `case default` runs.
conditions-3.prompt: Which operator means "not equal" in Fortran?
conditions-3.explain: Fortran writes "not equal" as `/=`. `!` starts a comment, so `!=` does not work.
conditions-4.explain: `.and.` needs both sides to be true. `b` is false, so the `else` block prints `no`.
conditions-5.explain: Fortran runs only the first block whose condition is true. `50 > 10` is already true, so the other conditions are not checked.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the condition so the code prints `Even`.
conditions-6.explain: `==` compares two values. `mod(8, 2)` is `0`, so the condition is true. `=` only stores values.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Other`.
conditions-7.explain: `case default` matches every value that no other `case` matches.
conditions-8.prompt: Build the first line of an if block that runs when `done` is false.
conditions-8.explain: `.not.` turns false into true. The condition goes in parentheses, and `then` ends the line.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints `Cold` when `t` is less than 10, and `Warm` otherwise.
conditions-9.explain: The `if` line opens the block, the code for a true condition follows, then `else` with the other code, and `end if` closes the block.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
conditions-10.pairs.3: at least one side is true
conditions-11.prompt: The program should print `Adult`. Which line has the bug?
conditions-11.explain: An `if` block needs `then` at the end of the line: `if (age >= 18) then`.
conditions-12.explain: An `if` block is closed with `end if`. A plain `end` would end the whole program.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with do loops and do while, and control loops with exit and cycle.
loops.lesson.0: `do i = 1, 3` … `end do` repeats the lines in between. The **loop variable** `i` must be a declared integer. It starts at `1` and goes up to `3`, and both ends are included.
loops.lesson.2: A third number sets the **step**: `do i = 0, 10, 5` counts `0`, `5`, `10`. A negative step counts down. When the start is already past the end, the loop runs zero times.
loops.lesson.4: A loop often builds up a result. Here `total` starts at `0`, and each round adds the current value of `i`.
loops.lesson.7: `do while (condition)` repeats as long as the condition is true. Fortran checks the condition before every round, so the loop can also run zero times.
loops.lesson.10: `exit` leaves the loop at once. `cycle` skips the rest of the current round and continues with the next one. A `do` with nothing after it repeats forever, until an `exit` stops it.
loops.lesson.13: Do not change the loop variable inside a `do i = …` loop: that is an error. In a `do while` loop, make sure that something inside the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
loops.card.0: `do i = 1, n` … `end do` counts from 1 to n
loops.card.2: `do while (x < 100)` repeats while the condition is true
loops.card.3: `exit` leaves the loop, `cycle` jumps to the next round
loops-2.explain: `n` goes `100`, `50`, `25`, `12`, `6`, `3`, `1`. That is 6 rounds, because integer division cuts off the decimal part.
loops-3.prompt: How many times does this print `Hi`?
loops-3.explain: Without a step, `do` counts up. `10` is already past `1`, so the loop runs zero times.
loops-4.explain: `cycle` skips the rest of the round when `i` is `3`. The loop then continues with `4` and `5`.
loops-5.statement: `exit` ends only the current round, and the loop continues with the next value.
loops-5.explain: `exit` leaves the whole loop. `cycle` is the statement that jumps to the next round.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, one number per line.
loops-6.explain: A step of `-1` counts down by one. With a step of `1`, the loop would run zero times.
loops-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `16`.
loops-8.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts `i` from 1 to 10.
loops-8.explain: A counting loop is `do`, the loop variable, `=`, then the start and the end separated by a comma.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints `24`, which is 1 * 2 * 3 * 4.
loops-9.explain: `f` must start at `1` before the loop. The loop multiplies it by `1`, `2`, `3` and `4`, and the result is printed after the loop.
loops-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-10.pairs.1: repeats while the condition is true
loops-11.explain: Fortran separates the start and the end with a comma: `do i = 1, 4`.
loops-12.prompt: The program should print 3, 2 and 1, one number per line. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: With `n > 1` the loop stops before it prints `1`. Write `do while (n > 0)`.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Store many values in one array, count indexes from 1, work on whole arrays at once and use sum, size and maxval.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** holds many values of the same type under one name. `integer :: scores(3)` declares an array of 3 integers. You reach one element with its **index** in parentheses. The first element is `scores(1)`, not `scores(0)`.
arrays.lesson.2: `[3, 1, 4, 1]` creates an array with these values, and older code writes it as `(/ 3, 1, 4, 1 /)`. `size(a)` gives the number of elements. The format `'(*(I0, :, 1X))'` prints all values in one line: `*` repeats the part in parentheses as often as needed, `1X` adds a space, and `:` stops when no values are left, so there is no space after the last number.
arrays.lesson.5: Calculations work on every element at once: `a * 2` doubles each element, and `a + b` adds two arrays of the same size element by element. `b = 10` stores `10` in every element of `b`.
arrays.lesson.7: Fortran has built-in functions for arrays: `sum(a)` adds all elements, `product(a)` multiplies them, and `maxval(a)` and `minval(a)` give the largest and the smallest element.
arrays.lesson.10: A `do` loop from `1` to `size(a)` visits every element. A **slice** such as `a(2:4)` is a part of the array, here the elements 2, 3 and 4. You can use a slice like a small array.
arrays.lesson.12: An index outside the array, such as `a(0)` or `a(6)` for an array of 5 elements, is an error. Fortran does not always stop with a message: the program may read or change wrong memory, so check your indexes.
arrays.card.0: `integer :: a(5)` has 5 elements, `a(1)` is the first
arrays.card.2: `a * 2` and `a + b` work on every element
arrays.card.4: `'(*(I0, :, 1X))'` prints all values in one line
arrays-1.explain: Indexes start at `1`, so `a(2)` is the second element, `8`.
arrays-3.explain: `a * 10` multiplies every element, so `a` becomes `40`, `50`, `60`. The third element is `60`.
arrays-4.statement: The first element of `integer :: a(5)` is `a(0)`.
arrays-4.explain: Fortran arrays start at index `1` unless you say otherwise. The elements are `a(1)` to `a(5)`.
arrays-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the number of elements, `3`.
arrays-5.explain: `size(a)` gives the number of elements. `sum(a)` would add them and print `24`.
arrays-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the largest element, `9`.
arrays-6.explain: `maxval(a)` returns the largest element of an array. `a(4)` is only the last element, `6`.
arrays-7.prompt: Build the declaration of an integer array `days` with 7 elements.
arrays-7.explain: The type comes first, then `::`, the name and the number of elements in parentheses.
arrays-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints 4, 8 and 12, one number per line.
arrays-8.explain: First the array gets its values, then every element is doubled, and then the loop prints the elements one by one.
arrays-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays-10.prompt: The program should print `First: 5`. Which line has the bug?
arrays-10.explain: The first element is `a(1)`. There is no `a(0)` in this array.
arrays-11.explain: An array of values is written with square brackets: `a = [1, 2, 3]`.
arrays-12.explain: `a(2:3)` is `3` and `4`. Adding `1` to every element gives `4` and `5`.
procedures.title: Functions and subroutines
procedures.summary: Split a program into functions and subroutines after contains, pass arguments with intent and return results.
procedures.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run many times. A **subroutine** does a task, and you start it with `call`. You write procedures after the word `contains`, at the end of the program and before `end program`.
procedures.lesson.2: The values in parentheses are **arguments**. You declare them inside the procedure. `character(len=*)` accepts a text of any length. `intent(in)` says that the procedure only reads the argument and does not change it.
procedures.lesson.4: A **function** calculates a value, and you use it inside an expression. `function square(x) result(y)` names the function, its argument `x` and its result variable `y`. You declare `y` inside the function and store the result in it.
procedures.lesson.6: A function can take several arguments, separated by commas. Here both arguments and the result are real numbers.
procedures.lesson.9: A subroutine can give values back through its arguments. With `intent(inout)` it reads the argument and may change it. With `intent(out)` it only sets the argument. You pass variables, and after the `call` they hold the new values.
procedures.lesson.12: Variables that you declare inside a procedure, such as `tmp`, are **local**: they exist only inside that procedure. The `implicit none` of the program also applies to the procedures after `contains`.
procedures.lesson.13: Changing an `intent(in)` argument is an error. Do not give a local variable a start value in its declaration, like `integer :: n = 0`, inside a procedure: Fortran sets it only once, not at every call. Use a separate line `n = 0` instead.
procedures.card.1: `function f(x) result(y)` returns the value of `y`
procedures-2.explain: With `intent(inout)`, the change to `n` goes back to `x`. So `x` is `15` after the call.
procedures-3.prompt: How do you run a subroutine named `report` that has no arguments?
procedures-3.explain: A subroutine is always started with `call`.
procedures-4.statement: You start a function with `call`, in the same way as a subroutine.
procedures-4.explain: A function returns a value, so you use it in an expression, such as `x = square(2)`. Only subroutines are started with `call`.
procedures-5.prompt: Complete the declaration so the subroutine only reads `n`.
procedures-5.explain: `intent(in)` means the subroutine reads the argument but does not change it. That also allows a fixed value such as `7` as the argument.
procedures-6.prompt: Complete the first line of the function so it returns `r`.
procedures-6.explain: The first line names the function and its arguments, and `result(r)` names the variable that holds the return value.
procedures-7.prompt: Build the line that runs the subroutine `move` with the arguments `x` and `y`, in this order.
procedures-7.explain: `call` starts a subroutine. The arguments go in parentheses, separated by commas.
procedures-8.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a complete program that prints Hello.
procedures-8.explain: The main code with `call` comes first. After `contains` follows the subroutine, and `end program` closes the whole program.
procedures-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
procedures-9.pairs.2: the argument is read and changed
procedures-10.prompt: The program should print `5`. Which line has the bug?
procedures-10.explain: `a` has `intent(in)` and must not change, and the result `s` never gets a value. Write `s = a + b`.
procedures-11.prompt: The program should print `9`. Which line has the bug?
procedures-11.explain: A subroutine is started with `call`: `call square(n)`.
procedures-12.options.3: Nothing, the program does not compile
procedures-12.explain: With `intent(out)`, the subroutine sets the argument, and the new value goes back to `a`.
types.title: Derived types and modules
types.summary: Group data in your own derived types, put types and procedures into modules and use them in a program.
types.lesson.0: A **derived type** groups several values into one new type. You define it with `type :: point` … `end type point`, and each value inside is a **component**. `type(point) :: p` declares a variable of the type, and `%` reaches a component: `p%x`.
types.lesson.2: `person("Ada", 36)` creates a value with all components, in the order of the type definition. `b = a` copies all components, so changing `b` later does not change `a`.
types.lesson.5: A **module** collects constants, types and procedures, so that many programs can share them. Here the module comes before the program in the same file. In the program, `use geometry` comes right after the `program` line, before `implicit none`.
types.lesson.7: Types and procedures work well together in a module. Here the subroutine `deposit` takes an `account` and changes its balance.
types.lesson.9: `use constants, only: g` makes only the listed names available. In bigger programs this shows clearly where each name comes from.
types.lesson.11: In bigger projects, each module goes into its own file, and the compiler translates it before the programs that use it. The order inside a program is always: `use` lines, `implicit none`, declarations, statements, and then `contains` with the procedures.
types.lesson.12: `use` must come before `implicit none` and before all declarations. Components are reached with `%`, not with a dot: write `p%x`, not `p.x`.
types.card.0: `type :: point` … `end type point` defines a type
types.card.1: `type(point) :: p` declares a variable, `p%x` is a component
types-1.explain: `box(3, 4)` sets `w` to `3` and `h` to `4`, and `3 * 4` is `12`.
types-2.explain: `start` is `10`. The inner `next` returns `11`, and the outer one returns `12`.
types-3.prompt: Which character reaches a component of a derived type, as in `p ? x`?
types-4.statement: In a program, `use` comes after `implicit none`.
types-4.explain: `use` lines come first, right after the `program` line. `implicit none` follows them.
types-5.prompt: Complete the program so it can call `hello` from the module.
types-5.explain: `use greetings` makes everything from the module `greetings` available in the program.
